title: The mobile visit for an accounting firm
metaTitle: Accounting firm mobile website, first screen
excerpt: An accounting firm mobile website should show who does the work, for whom, and how to book a call on the first phone screen. Build that before the desktop.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table, a single worker on a small surface the way a founder will meet the site on a phone.
caption: One person, one laptop, a table small enough to feel like a real visit. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first phone screen?
faqs.answer: The name of who does the work, the kind of company they do it for, and a button to book a call. One face can sit with that sentence if it does not push the words off the screen. A skyline, the word excellence, and a long menu can wait.

faqs.question: Why do desktop accounting sites fail on a phone?
faqs.answer: A wide hero often stacks the photograph above the sentence, so the founder sees a city before a person. Fee tables and hover menus do not survive a thumb. Write the narrow screen first, and let the wide layout borrow from it.

faqs.question: How should booking work on a phone?
faqs.answer: Use one primary control that says book a call, large enough to tap, with a line about what the call is. Keep client log-in visually secondary. If you ask for details, keep them to name, email, company type, and the question, with labels that stay visible.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An accounting firm mobile website has to finish the introduction on the first screen of a phone. Show who does the work and for whom, and show a way to book a call. Do not let the desktop composition decide that screen. A founder who needs a calm expert is often checking you between other work, on a small display, with the ledger still open in another app.

W3C's overview of WCAG is explicit that the guidelines cover mobile. Google's Core Web Vitals ask for Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Those numbers are felt more sharply on a phone. A layout that only balances when the window is wide fails the founder you wrote the page for.

## Put the person on the first screen

Start with a phone-width frame and the decision only.

Who, in text, large enough to read without pinching. "Mina Alvarez closes the books for owner-led studios." For whom has to be in that same breath. A second company type can follow as a line underneath if you truly serve two. A list of eight industries cannot.

Book a call, as a button with those words, visible without a menu. If a sticky bar holds it, the bar must not cover the name. A bar that hides Mina in order to advertise a meeting with Mina is a muddle.

One picture, cropped so the face survives. Not a skyline reduced to a gray stripe above the fold. If the photograph pushes the name below the first screen, move the photograph under the sentence. The face supports the words. It does not replace them.

Leave excellence, the city, and the award row off that screen. They can live lower if they are true. They are not the sort. A founder in ten seconds, the window Nielsen Norman Group describes as the harsh first judgment, needs the person and the company type. They can meet your taste after they know they are in the right place.

Read it out loud on the device. If you must scroll to learn who and how to book, the desktop file has already won.

## What a wide layout breaks when it stacks

Teams polish the laptop version, then stack the blocks. The stack looks logical and still fails.

A hero with the skyline on the left and the sentence on the right will stack the skyline first. The founder sees a city. Mina waits below. Put the words first in the document order. Let the wide layout place the photo beside them only when there is room.

A header with a logo, six services, a client login, a phone number, and a button will not fit. On a phone it becomes a cramped bar or a menu that hides the booking. Keep the phone header to the firm name and "Book a call." Put the jobs in a short menu, or let the page be the list, with targets a thumb can hit.

Hover menus do not exist here. If monthly books are only under a hover called "Solutions," they are missing. Every job you want is a tap.

Fee tables designed as wide grids collapse into an unreadable smear. Restack each shape as a heading, one sentence, and two short lists. A services page of three columns becomes a sequence of blocks with the outcome first. An about page of tiny faces becomes names large enough to recognize, with the company type under each name.

Fixed layers add up. A cookie banner, a chat bubble, a sticky header, and a sticky footer can cover the name and the button. Keep one persistent control, the booking. Let the rest wait until the founder has seen who the firm is.

## The call has to be easy to start

WCAG 2.2 includes a minimum target size of 24 by 24 CSS pixels for pointer inputs, with spacing exceptions. Treat that as a floor. The booking button should be larger, with space so a thumb does not open the menu or the client login by mistake.

The login for existing clients is the usual mobile mix-up. It is useful, and it should look secondary. A founder who taps "log in" and hits a wall thinks you are a software product. Label it "Client log in" and keep "Book a call" as the primary control in the first view.

If a short form sits on the homepage, ask for a name, an email, the kind of company, and the question. Label every field in text that stays visible. Use the email keyboard for email. WCAG's principles, perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, show up as labels and a form that can be finished with a thumb. Do not ask for last year's file, a company number, and a paragraph of history before anyone has agreed to talk. Those can follow the booking.

Say what the call is, next to the button. Thirty minutes, or whatever is true, to see if the person, the company type, and the timing fit. The confirmation screen should repeat that, and say whether the calendar is confirmed or a person still accepts it. Silence after a tap feels like a lost request.

If you publish a phone number, put hours beside it. A number that only works at a desk should not be the thing a mobile header screams. If the real next step is a video call, the button should say that, so nobody travels across town for a conversation you meant to hold online.

## Speed and a steady page

Test on a phone on an ordinary connection, held in the hand. The name and the button should be readable while images finish. If the only version of the sentence is baked into a photograph of a skyline, the founder waits for the costume before they can read. Put the words in text.

Ship the portrait at the size the phone displays so LCP can land within 2.5 seconds. Give it dimensions so the button does not jump, keeping CLS under 0.1. A late chat widget that shoves the booking is both a layout shift and a hit to INP, which Google wants under 200 milliseconds. Maps of the office can wait on the contact page, and only if visiting matters before the call. Many of these relationships are video. Do not make the founder download a map to book a video call.

Reduced motion matters. If the hero pans across a city, provide a still for people who asked the system to reduce motion. The person did not need to drift sideways to be credible.

When you change the portrait, version the file. A cached skyline beside a new sentence is a contradiction delivered by the phone's memory.

## A hallway review

Use one phone and one person who did not design the page.

1. Load the homepage on a cellular connection.
2. Without scrolling, say who does the work, for what kind of company, and how to book.
3. Tap the booking. Complete it with a thumb, make one mistake, and fix it without zooming.
4. Open monthly books, or whatever the lead job is, from the menu. The heading should match the label.
5. Confirm the client login is not the thing you hit by accident.

If step 2 fails, reorder the first screen before you debate the type. If step 3 fails, shorten the form. If the menu and the heading disagree, fix the words. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds when the value is unclear. Step 2 is that test.

Repeat after visual polish. Skylines grow back when a desktop review feels empty without them.

## Pages that get the same treatment

The pricing page, the services page, and the contact page are often opened from search straight onto a phone. Each still needs a person or a job, and a booking the thumb can hit.

A pricing page leads with the shape, not a spreadsheet. A services block leads with the outcome and the boundary. An about page leads with the name. The contact page tells them what happens after they book, how fast, and what to have in mind. Entity, ledger, the question. A glass-building gallery is optional. The reply path is not.

## When the laptop review disagrees with the phone

Partners often approve the site on a conference-room display. Ask them to review on their own phones, brightness ordinary, no one narrating. The skyline will shrink. The button will look obvious or missing. Believe the phone.

Keep a careful wide layout if you want it. It is the second version. The phone version has to show who, for whom, and how to book a call without making the founder hunt. Build that, then let the wide page borrow.

The contact path is where a mobile founder either finishes or gives up. Read [what the contact page has to explain](/blog/a-contact-path-for-an-accounting-firm) before you add fields copied from a paper intake form.

When you want a second look at a first screen that has to work in the hand, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the page on your phone, not a slide of the desktop.
